paper_title: Mind2Act World: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Embodied Mind, Physical Action, and Mind-Action Composition in Robotic Manipulation

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Embodied intelligence aims to let robots perform complex physical tasks with human-like adaptability and reliability, which requires three complementary capabilities: history-based cognitive reasoning, precise and timely physical execution, and the composition of reasoning and execution through environmental feedback. Yet existing benchmarks either evaluate reasoning and execution within the same tasks or assess them separately without their composition, so they reveal little about whether a failure comes from reasoning, execution, or their composition. We introduce Mind2Act World, a diagnostic benchmark of 30 simulated manipulation tasks from five real-world application domains. Each task has three difficulty levels and two scene settings (Clean and Random), yielding 180 configurations. The tasks form three views: Mind tests decisions based on past observations, Act tests precise and timely execution, and Mind2Act combines both in closed-loop tasks where action outcomes guide later decisions. Comparing the three views shows whether a system lacks a capability or fails to compose capabilities it already has. A diagnosis harness further attributes the failed episodes of three representative systems to Mind, Act, or their composition and summarizes each system in a profile card. Our evaluation of multimodal agents, vision-language-action models (VLAs), and world-action models (WAMs) shows that competence in a single view does not carry over to Mind2Act tasks. Even the strongest agent succeeds in 52.7% of Mind and 39.0% of Act episodes but in only 12.0% of Mind2Act episodes. The strongest agent retains task state but struggles with sustained contact, whereas end-to-end policies execute practiced motions but retain little task state. These findings point to composing reasoning and execution through environmental feedback as the main open problem.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Knowledge is the beginning of action and action is the completion of knowledge. Wang Yangming The central ambition of embodied intelligence is to enable robots to perform complex physical tasks with human-like adaptability and reliability. Studies of human sensorimotor control indicate that adaptive and reliable manipulation involves reasoning over task-relevant information, executing physical actions precisely, and adapting behavior through environmental feedback [13]. In the cooking task of Fig. 1, robot must remember which ingredient to add next, coordinate both arms to add the ingredient, and switch the stove from heating to keep-warm mode based on temperature feedback. These requirements motivate three capabilities. Mind decides what to do from earlier observations. Act produces the required physical effect in time. Mind-Action Composition closes the loop, so that remembered information guides each action and each physical outcome updates the next decision. Recent embodied systems spanning multimodal agents [32], vision-language-action models (VLAs) [19, 20], world-action models (WAMs) [23, 26], and hybrid architectures [27, 28] have substantially advanced robotic manipulation. However, their capabilities in Mind, Act, and Mind-Action Composition remain poorly understood, which makes it difficult to identify capability bottlenecks and guide further development. Two limitations of existing embodied benchmarks [4, 68, 12] explain why. First, conventional benchmarks often assess cognitive reasoning and physical execution within the same tasks and report only whether task succeeds [46], so failure cannot be traced to Mind or Act. Second, although recent benchmarks have introduced finer-grained diagnostics and separate assessments of reasoning and physical execution [8, 11 13], they rarely evaluate Mind-Action Composition, particularly whether physical outcomes can effectively inform subsequent decisions. Closing this gap requires tasks that stress one capability while keeping the others present but easy, judgment of composition based on verified physical outcomes, and comparison of systems with different action interfaces and inference speeds on equal terms. To this end, we introduce Mind2Act World, diagnostic benchmark for Mind, Act, and Mind-Action Composition in robotic manipulation  (Fig. 1)  . Its 30 tasks come from five real-world application domains and are organized into three views of ten tasks each, covering 12 capability categories. Each view emphasizes one demand by design. Mind tasks keep physical operations simple, Act tasks state the Research preprint mmlab@SIGS required operation explicitly, and Mind2Act tasks chain dependent operations so that each physical outcome decides what comes next. Success is judged from physical predicates on the environment, and the evaluator records stages and events within each episode. Each task has three difficulty levels that raise its demands while keeping the objective fixed. Each level runs in Clean and Random scene, which share the same instance but differ in clutter, materials and lighting (180 configurations in total). Agents and end-to-end policies share the same tasks, information contract and evaluator, and 4,500 demonstrations (75.8 hours) are provided for fine-tuning end-to-end policies. diagnosis harness combines rule-based analysis of the evaluators stage and event records with an LLM judge to attribute each failed episode of three representative systems to Mind, Act, or their composition. It summarizes each of these systems in per-model report called model profile card (Fig. 6; Appendix E.4). Our evaluation on Mind2Act World reveals clear pattern. Existing architectures are uneven across Mind and Act, yet all struggle with Mind-Action Composition. The strongest agent retains task state well but struggles to sustain contact, and its timed successes are measured with simulator that pauses during inference. End-to-end policies respond within fraction of second and execute practiced motions, but retain little task state, and the memory of the VLAs largely disappears under scene randomization. Notably, on Mind2Act, the strongest system succeeds in only 12.0% of episodes, far below its 52.7% on Mind and 39.0% on Act, and no end-to-end policy exceeds 3.6%. Competence in either capability therefore does not carry over to Mind2Act tasks. The contributions of this work are summarized as follows: We introduce Mind2Act World, diagnostic benchmark comprising 30 manipulation tasks grounded in real-world requirements. Organized into three views, it systematically evaluates Mind, Act, and Mind-Action Composition. We develop diagnosis harness that combines rule-based analysis with an LLM judge to identify the stage at which each failed episode first breaks down and to attribute the failure to Mind, Act, or Mind-Action Composition. The harness also summarizes three representative models in model profile cards of their failure patterns and behavioral tendencies. We evaluate representative multimodal agents, VLAs, and WAMs on shared tasks and scoring, with separate leaderboards for agents and end-to-end policies. Our results show that systems differ in which of Mind and Act is weaker, and that all of them struggle with Mind-Action Composition.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: 2.1 Embodied Policies and Agents Robot manipulation policies have evolved from imitation learning [1517] to large-scale generalist policies. Vision-language-action models such as OpenVLA [19], 𝜋0.5 [20], RDT2 [21] and G0.5 [22] improve instruction following and cross-task transfer, while world-action models such as LDA-1B [24], Motus [25] and DreamZero [26] couple predictive modeling with control. Agent-based systems take different route, turning language-model reasoning into executable programs [32] and feeding success detection back into planning [67, 68]. Recent work also addresses memory-augmented manipulation [29, 30, 55], dynamic manipulation [61, 62], and forceor tactile-aware control [65, 66]. Despite this progress, each line is usually evaluated where only its own demand is hard: memory methods on tasks with simple execution, dynamic and contact-aware controllers on tasks whose target is given, and agents on tasks where perceiving the outcome is assumed. In practice, failure may come from holding the wrong task state, missing the intended physical effect, or continuing without checking that the effect occurred. Mind2Act World therefore makes all three demands hard within the same tasks and evaluates agents, VLAs and WAMs on them. Research preprint 4 mmlab@SIGS Table 1. Comparison with existing benchmarks. RLBench [5], CALVIN [33] and LIBERO [4] cover multi-task, language-conditioned and lifelong settings. RoboTwin 2.0 [34] evaluates bimanual generalization, and THE COLOSSEUM [48] stresses distribution shift. BEHAVIOR-1K [7] and RoboCasa [6] pose long household activities. Memory benchmarks such as RMBench [31] and RoboMME [38] isolate history-dependent decisions, the latter with Easy, Medium and Hard levels and timed stopping of moving objects. GeoMind [36] evaluates spatial reasoning and spatial memory through structured manipulation tasks, with controlled scene variations and diagnostic metrics for spatial understanding and execution failures. RoboDojo [8] and RobotWorld [9] diagnose capability dimensions with stage scores or execution traces, and real-world benchmarks such as RoboArena [41] Research preprint 5 mmlab@SIGS assess deployed policies. For agents built on foundation models, EmbodiedBench [52] spans high-level and low-level embodied tasks, and Embodied Playground [11] evaluates closed-loop behavior in which earlier actions set up later prerequisites. X2Real [12] records subtask failure nodes, separates reasoning from manipulation dimensions including dynamic operation, and compares VLA, WAM and agent routes. RoboColiseum [13] reports gap between task understanding and reliable execution. RLE-Bench [10] and Embodied First Exam [14] instead evaluate agents that write and iterate on code to solve robot control and robot learning engineering problems. Most of these benchmarks entangle reasoning and execution within one task, so failure cannot be attributed to either, or measure them in separate evaluations, leaving open whether they hold together when one realized outcome sets the conditions for the next decision. Mind2Act World addresses this gap by deriving tasks from real-world requirements and organizing them into Mind, Act and Mind2Act views with graded difficulty, so that the same demands are measured in isolation and in composition across architectures. Table 1 compares Mind2Act World with 21 representative simulation benchmarks. Mind2Act World tasks also have long horizons, with training demonstrations averaging 60.7 overall and 99.6 in the Mind2Act view. Demonstrations in RoboTwin 2.0, RoboDojo, MIKASA-Robo-VLA and RoboCasa365 average 13 to 40 s, and only BEHAVIOR-1K, whose tasks are full household activities, has longer ones.

sections.title: 3 Mind2Act World Benchmark
sections.content: Mind2Act World asks whether failures in manipulation tasks arise from incorrect reasoning, imprecise execution, or poor composition of the two. The benchmark comprises 30 simulation tasks on bimanual ARX X5 platform, organized into 3 views that place different demands on system. Mind focuses on history-dependent reasoning, Act emphasizes constrained physical execution, and Mind2Act focuses on their composition. Each task has Easy, Medium, and Hard levels, and each level is evaluated in Clean and Random scene setting, yielding 180 configurations. Fig. 2 presents an overview of our 30 tasks. The following sections describe the design principles (Section 3.1), task views (Section 3.2), difficulty levels (Section 3.3), training data (Section 3.4), and evaluation setting (Section 3.5). 3.1 Design Principles Four principles guide the benchmark design: (i) build tasks from real-world requirements, (ii) evaluate reasoning and execution capabilities separately and in combination, (iii) verify physical outcomes and record task progress, and (iv) support evaluation across different model architectures. (i) Tasks are built from real-world requirements. Embodied agents in industry, homes, and service settings must follow instructions across multiple stages and produce the required physical effects at the right time. We construct tasks in three steps. First, we identify practical requirement, such as remembering orders after they leave view, maintaining target instrument reading, intercepting objects on conveyor, or responding to appliance feedback. We then reproduce this requirement in tabletop scene and define completion conditions based on physical outcomes. Table 2 groups the tasks into five application domains: home and food service, manufacturing and logistics, instrument operation and dexterous tool use, assembly and physical reasoning, and companion and edutainment. It also identifies the industrial or service requirement behind each task. In the companion and edutainment domain, structured activities such as card matching and paddle ball represent cognitive and sports training for older adults and children. All thirty tasks are tabletop abstractions of such needs. They isolate the requirement that makes the activity hard for robot and do not reproduce deployed workflow in full. (ii) Capabilities are decoupled, then recoupled. Long-horizon tasks often combine memory, planning, precision, and timing, making the source of failure difficult to identify. Mind2Act World evaluates these demands through three views with related task semantics. Mind tasks require only routine execution, so they examine how system maintains and uses task state. Act tasks specify the required operation to examine its physical execution ability. Mind2Act tasks combine these demands and test composition in both directions. The views define observable task demands, not internal policy modules. Each view emphasizes one demand without removing the other. Mind task still requires routine grasping and placing, and an Act task still requires Research preprint 7 mmlab@SIGS reading the cue that it responds to. Strong performance on the separate demands with weak performance on their combination is therefore consistent with composition problem. Because the views contain different tasks and Mind2Act workflows are also longer, view-level differences do not by themselves identify composition failures (Section 5.2). Matched interventions are left to future work (Section 7). (iii) Outcomes are physically verified and traced within the episode. Task scores depend on simulator states and events. deposit counts only after an object is released and supported at the target. dial reading must remain stable after release, and key strike must produce an effective press. The task records also distinguish incorrect decisions from failed execution, such as selecting the wrong object versus failing to place the correct one. Partial-progress scores and event records show which stages were completed and where the first observable error occurred. (iv) Evaluation is architecture-agnostic. The benchmark supports comparisons across architectures using shared tasks, instances, and scoring rules. End-to-end policies act from observations after training on the shared demonstrations; agents act through declared motion tools. Section 4 specifies what each interface exposes, so that differences in performance can be read against differences in information and control. 3.2 Task Design Task design follows the three views introduced above. Mind tests decisions that depend on earlier information (Section 3.2.1). Act tests whether specified operation produces the required physical effect within spatial and temporal constraints (Section 3.2.2). Mind2Act tests their composition across dependent operations (Section 3.2.3). Within each view, tasks are grouped by capability. The following subsections explain each category through representative tasks and describe the failures it can reveal. Appendix Table 20 lists all tasks, their source workflows, categories, and difficulty variables. Appendix provides the full specifications. 3.2.1 Mind: Reasoning over Long-Horizon Dependencies decision may depend on information that is no longer visible, such as part on an earlier tray, the effect of an unlabeled control, or the portion of an order already served. These dependencies require system to retain evidence and update task state throughout an episode. Many end-to-end visuomotor policies use only the current observation or short history of recent frames [15, 16, 19, 20]. Recent memory-augmented policies have begun to address this limitation [29, 30, 55, 56]. Mind tasks examine whether system can make correct decisions after relevant cues disappear, while requiring only routine execution. Memory categories. The ten Mind tasks cover five memory categories, with two tasks per category. The categories differ in how earlier information supports later decisions. Entity memory retains an objects identity or an associated value when its current appearance is insufficient. Feedback-rule learning uses interaction to infer and retain rule or hidden configuration. Examples include learning the effects of unlabeled controls and recovering an arrangement from feedback that reports only the number of correct positions. Process memory tracks completed operations and their order, such as fulfilled requests or the original order of disassembled layers. Spatial memory retains locations when reference frame moves or map is hidden. Integrated memory combines identity, location, and order, as in tracking covered workpiece or matching cards revealed two at time. Difficulty increases the information to retain, such as bindings, layers, hazard cells, card pairs, or exchanges, while keeping precision demands low. Representative cases. We demonstrate representative cases in Fig. 3. In workpiece tracking and route replay (M1), the robot remembers the target location and station route, tracks the hidden target through cover exchanges, and retrieves it to visit the required stations in order. This tests integrated memory of identity, location, and sequence. In steamer-stack order restoration (P2), the robot observes each baskets contents as it unstacks the baskets, then restores their original order and replaces the lid. On Hard, distractor baskets have identical exteriors but different contents. The robot must retain the original Research preprint 8 mmlab@SIGS layer order and select the correct baskets, testing process memory. What Mind diagnoses. Mind task records distinguish decision errors from execution errors, such as choosing the wrong item versus failing to place the correct one. Because execution is routine, an error on Mind task usually comes from the task state system maintains. 3.2.2 Act: Dynamic Response and Precise Physical Execution Correct decisions must be translated into physical effects that meet spatial and temporal constraints. Common examples include intercepting conveyor objects, passing through cyclic gates, maintaining instrument readings, carrying loose loads, and folding fabric. Act tasks specify what to do and evaluate how it is executed. Act provides reference for execution demands that also occur in Mind2Act workflows, such as conveyor pickup in meal assembly. This allows performance on separate operations to be compared with performance in dependent workflow. Execution categories. Dynamic response concerns the timing of an actions effect relative to changing scene. Examples include intercepting objects before they leave the reachable region, pressing button within cue window, and passing through cyclic gate before it closes. Dynamic stability adds related demand. The robot must control its own motion without disturbing carried load, such as loose balls on tray. Timing follows the simulation clock, which pauses during inference. Precise physical execution concerns spatial accuracy, contact, and stability. It includes setting instrument readings, maintaining tool contact along path, controlling stamp orientation, folding cloth that remains flat after release, and spacing dominoes to complete physical chain to bell. Difficulty increases through shorter time windows, additional obstacles or loads, tighter tolerances, and less controllable materials or shapes. Representative cases. Cases are demonstrated in Fig. 3. In domino chain to bell (PR6), the robot places dominoes upright along curved band and pushes the first to trigger chain that rings bell. This requires precise spacing and orientation so that contact propagates through the chain. Difficulty increases with more dominoes, greater height variation, and larger band span. In tray carrying with loose balls (DR4), the robot carries loose balls on tray past obstacles while keeping each ball within its marked circle. This tests dynamic stability, as the robot must control tray motion to preserve the positions of the balls throughout transport. What Act diagnoses. Act tasks assess endpoint accuracy, stability after release, contact continuity, and timing. By limiting long-horizon reasoning demands, they provide reference for interpreting execution failures in Mind2Act workflows. 3.2.3 Mind2Act: Composition across Dependent Operations Mind2Act evaluates how reasoning and execution interact across workflow. Retained information, such as an order, layout, or recipe sequence, determines the next operation and its execution requirements. Each physical outcome then changes the task state on which later decisions depend. system may handle the separate demands yet struggle to combine them over time. Mind2Act therefore focuses on outcome-conditioned continuation, that is, choosing subsequent actions from the state produced by earlier operations. Each task combines memory or reasoning demand with physical execution demand, as listed in Appendix Table 20. Composition mechanisms. The tasks cover five composition mechanisms. In cumulative progress (CP01, CP03), remaining demand or slot occupancy determines the next operation. Progress advances only after successful delivery or stable plate placement. In state-dependent prerequisites and repair (CP02, CP08, CP09), later operations require valid physical state. The robot may need to stop turntable before covering cake, rebuild misplaced base to match remembered blueprint, or redraw original strokes removed during erasing. In feedback-driven adjustment (CP04, CP06), temperature or balance-beam Research preprint 9 mmlab@SIGS deflection guides the next operation. In sequence and plan execution (CP05, CP07), remembered sequence or construction plan determines the order of operations. Progress requires effective strikes or stable placements; CP07 also requires toy car to cross the completed bridge. In predictive decision under time pressure (CP10), the robot applies fixed color rule to each incoming ball: return white ball and let red ball pass. It must select and time its response before the ball arrives. Representative cases. In rotating-cake decoration (CP02), the robot remembers briefly shown macaron layout and reproduces it on rotating cake. It must stop the turntable and verify that the cake is stationary before placing the cover. In temperature-controlled cooking (CP04), the robot adds ingredients in the remembered recipe order, then uses temperature feedback to switch from HEAT to KEEP WARM within the required time window. Bridge building for toy car (CP07) requires selecting suitable parts and executing construction plan. The assembled bridge must remain stable after release and support the car as it crosses the gap, linking plan execution to physical test of the completed structure. In whiteboard restoration (CP09), the robot compares the current board with remembered drawing to identify added strokes. It must erase these strokes and redraw any original content removed during erasing, so that the final board matches the remembered colors, shapes, and layout. What Mind2Act diagnoses. Mind2Act examines whether system uses retained information to guide execution and updates that information from physical outcomes. Comparisons across views, supported by stage and event records, help identify composition failures. Difficulty inside the process. Task difficulty often arises during intermediate operations. Fig. 3 shows four steps from each of eight Hard-level demonstrations, two Mind, two Act and four Mind2Act tasks. At Hard, M1 involves seven cover exchanges, two of them irrelevant, and P2 involves four steamer tiers and two identical decoys. PR6 involves nine dominoes of mixed sizes along 76 cm curved band, and DR4 involves four loose balls, two pillars and marked circle of 20 mm radius. CP02 shows its sample for 3 s, CP04 involves bimanual jar handling and switch from HEAT to KEEP WARM within 2 of the pot reaching 80 C, CP07 uses 13 of 28 parts across 36 cm river, and CP09 requires uncapping pens with both hands. Failures in these intermediate operations can prevent later stages from succeeding, so we report stage progress alongside final success (Section 4.3). 3.3 Difficulty Design Aggregate scores can obscure the conditions under which performance declines. We therefore define three difficulty levels for each task. The objective remains fixed, while memory load, reasoning demands, precision, timing, or workflow dependencies increase. Easy tests the core requirement under the least demanding conditions. Medium increases the information to retain, the required precision, or the number of operations. Hard introduces greater demands through tighter constraints, longer dependent sequences, or combinations of these factors. The levels define progression within each task rather than common numerical scale across tasks. Comparing success and partial-progress scores across the three levels shows how performance on the same task changes as its demands increase. Fig. 4 illustrates these variations. sections.title: 4 Technical Implementation and Evaluation Protocol
sections.content: Systems that act through different interfaces must face the same scenes, the same clock and the same notion of success. Building on the task design in Section 3, this section describes how policies connect to the tasks, how an episode is executed and timed, and how its outcome is scored and protected against shortcuts. Appendix collects the implementation details needed for reproduction. 4.1 Platform and Policy Interfaces Comparing agents and end-to-end policies requires platform that both can drive and that produces the same physical effects for both. We implement Mind2Act World in Isaac Sim with two ARX X5 arms and parallel grippers. fixed head camera captures the scene layout, while two wrist cameras capture local gripperobject interactions. RGB images are rendered at 640 480 for all cameras. Task scenes combine shared robot and workspace assets with task-specific objects and mechanisms as depicted in Fig. 7. Their geometry, motion, and contact properties are configured to reproduce the physical effects required by each task. All systems follow common information contract detailed in Appendix B. Policies receive the task instruction, selected RGB views, and declared robot state. History access is limited to information previously exposed within the same episode. Hidden simulator state is accessible only to the evaluator. This includes unannounced parameters used for scoring, such as the numerical target angle and tolerance in PR5, gate timing in DR3, and allowable ball drift in DR4. The benchmark supports two action interfaces. End-to-end policies predict joint or end-effector actions. These predictions are converted to joint targets, and configured number of actions is executed from each chunk before the next prediction. Agents are multimodal language models that issue structured tool calls. The move_eef tool accepts an end-effector pose target and gripper command. The backend handles inverse kinematics and motion planning. The wait_steps tool advances simulation while maintaining the current arm and gripper targets. Agents can use memory_resolve to retrieve previously observed image by its observation identifier and add it to the models context. Retrieval does not advance simulation. An agent can also call give_up to end the episode itself. Every evaluated agent uses this one fixed harness of tools, planner and history access. Reset restores the robot, objects, task stage, evaluator, and random-number state. Policy memory is cleared between episodes and retained across stages within an episode. Physics simulation advances at 120 Hz, while arm and gripper targets are updated at 30 Hz. Simulation pauses during model inference. Task deadlines use simulation time, while inference latency and total runtime use wall-clock time, the elapsed real time. delayed model response therefore consumes wall-clock time without reducing the simulated response window, so timed tasks measure responses in simulation time rather than real-time performance. For end-to-end policies, each task and difficulty level has an episode horizon set to 1.2 times the 90th percentile of demonstration durations, rounded up to control step. An episode stopped by one is scored like any other unfinished episode. Episodes end on completion, policy termination, or budget exhaustion. As descriptive reference for composition, we also compare systems Mind2Act success rate with the product of its Mind and Act success rates, the value expected if Mind2Act workflow required one independent success of each kind. The task score is defined in Appendix B.3, and per-task success predicates are listed in Appendix F.2. 4.4 Evaluation Integrity Because an agent can declare that it has finished and policy can repeat an action until something happens, the evaluator has to judge outcomes. Completion is therefore assessed using environment-side Research preprint mmlab@SIGS predicates. Commands and success declarations receive credit only when the required physical conditions are met. Repeating an action earns credit only when it satisfies new requirement. Task rules distinguish irreversible failures, unscored actions, and valid exploration. For example, in DR4, ball leaving its circle causes failure even if it later rolls back. In F2, submitting an incomplete layout does not consume an attempt. In M2, revealing mismatched pair is valid exploration. sections.title: 5 Benchmark Results
sections.content: Building on the protocol in Section 4, we evaluate nine systems that span the two main routes to embodied manipulation: multimodal agents that act through tools and end-to-end policies trained on demonstrations. Section 5.1 describes the systems and the evaluation procedure. Section 5.2 analyzes how well they reason, act and compose the two, where and why they fall short across views, conditions and application domains, and what the evaluation costs in time and money. Section 5.3 summarizes which system suits which task. 5.1 Experimental Setup 5.1.1 Systems We evaluate two system families, each ranked on its own leaderboard. Agents are multimodal language models that select motion tools from camera images and robot state, without any training on Mind2Act World. We evaluate GPT-6 Astra [70], DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash [71] and Gemini-4-Argon [72]. End-to-end policies map observations and the instruction to robot actions after fine-tuning on the shared demonstrations. We evaluate the VLAs KinRT [73], 𝜋0.5 [20], G0.5 [22] and X-VLA [74], and the WAMs InternW0 [76] and FastWAM [75]. Appendix lists the evaluated systems. 5.1.2 Training and Adaptation We fine-tune each end-to-end policy from its public checkpoint on the shared collection of 4,500 demonstrations, fifty per task and difficulty level (Section 3.4.2), with the initialization, global batch size, and training steps of each system detailed in Appendix C. In contrast, we use the agents directly as provided through their APIs, without fine-tuning. 5.1.3 Inference and Evaluation Instances All evaluations run at 120 Hz physics and 30 Hz control/RGB observations, with simulation paused during inference so that task deadlines are measured in simulation time and inference cost in wall-clock time. Across the 180 configurations (30 tasks 3 levels 2 settings), the nine evaluated systems account for 56,700 scored episodes. At the start of an episode, each system receives the English task instruction, selected camera views, and declared robot state. End-to-end policies generate action chunks that are converted to robot targets at 30 Hz, whereas agents issue pose-level motion-tool requests and may retrieve earlier observations from the same episode. For each task and difficulty level, we fix shared list of 50 instances and evaluate them in both Clean and Random settings  (Table 3)  . End-to-end policies run on all 100 resulting episodes per task and level (9,000 episodes per policy), while agents run on shared subset of 5 Clean and 5 Random episodes (900 episodes per agent). Random instances preserve the underlying task instance while adding table clutter, one of 23 table materials, and one of six light types (with RGB channels scaled in [0, 2] and intensity in [0.8, 1.2]). The range is deliberately wide, so Random serves as an appearance stress test. End-to-end policies are allotted Research preprint mmlab@SIGS simulation-time horizon of 1.2 the 90th percentile of demonstration durations, shared across Clean and Random, with 2-hour wall-clock safety limit. Agents receive 4 this physics budget, up to 150 decisions per episode, and 6-hour wall-clock safety limit. All three agents are evaluated at medium reasoning effort. Mind2Act workflows mostly end at their first steps, before reasoning and execution ever have to work together. Reliable composition therefore first requires each capability to hold up at every step of workflow, which no current system achieves. Together they show that agents and end-to-end policies currently handle different kinds of task demand. Agents for reasoning-heavy steps. strong agent is suited to the steps of task that turn on what was seen before and on what to do next. GPT-6 Astra remembers and reasons well (52.7% on Mind), keeps that memory when the scene changes, and solves tasks whose target can be read and reached in few deliberate moves. Its limits lie in contact and timing. It completes none of the five contact-rich tasks, and its timed successes are measured with simulator that waits for it. The other two agents use the same tools yet differ widely on Mind, so this profile is specific to the model. End-to-end policies for execution-heavy steps. End-to-end policies are suited to steps that one practiced motion can cover. The four evaluated VLAs retain 8694% of their Act successes under scene randomization, and each has its own strength: G0.5 on timed reactions, X-VLA on resistance adjustment and cloth folding, and KinRT and 𝜋0.5 on memory, where the VLAs show little. They retain almost no task state, so any step that depends on earlier information is better left to another system. World-action models differ widely. InternW0 is the only end-to-end policy whose memory survives scene changes, and it nearly matches the agent on the blueprint task. It still follows its learned sequence without checking preconditions, as in cooking. FastWAM drops in both views under scene randomization, so this advantage is not inherent to world-action models. Some demands are met by no system yet. No evaluated system succeeds on M1, and GPT-6 Astra completes no episode of P2. sections.title: 6 Diagnostic Analysis
sections.content: Success rates measure task completion, and task scores measure partial progress. But they cannot identify where or why system fails within an episode, which is what model developers need to know. In this section, we examine where tasks fail, which errors recur across systems, and how these findings inform improvement priorities. Episode-level diagnosis and model profile cards (Section 6.1) connect failure patterns to task progress, budget use, and stopping decisions (Section 6.2), and the failure codes point to directions for improvement (Section 6.3). Inference latency, runtime and API cost are analyzed alongside success rates in Section 5.2. 6.1 Diagnosis Harness and Model Profile Cards Diagnosis harness design. We classify failures by the first unrecoverable error identified in the episode, using 21 failure codes (Appendix E.1). Mind errors concern perception and task reasoning, Act errors concern physical execution, and composition errors concern using physical outcomes to guide subsequent actions. Three episode-level codes capture timeouts, stalls, and cases with insufficient evidence. The label follows the observed error, regardless of the tasks view. Mind failure involves an error in perception or task reasoning. Examples include selecting the wrong object based on misremembered order (M-MEMORY) and incorrectly predicting how the scene will change (M-PREDICT). An Act failure occurs when the system selects an appropriate action but executes it incorrectly. Examples include losing grasp (A-GRASP) and executing the correct action too early or too late (A-TIMING). composition failure occurs when the system proceeds without verifying required outcome or fails to update its next action based on feedback. For example, the system may continue pressing the same button after the light cue changes (C-NO-UPDATE). The harness combines three layers of review as in Fig. 9a. First, deterministic rules use scorer outputs and simulator events to isolate the failure or bound the step at which it occurred. For cases left open by rules, an LLM judge inspects the video and action or tool-call history without overturning rule-based verdicts, flagging ambiguous cases as uncertain. Finally, human reviewers settle the cases the judge marks as uncertain. Fig. 9 shows the workflow on an illustrative example, and Appendix E.4 reports the results of this procedure for every failed episode of three representative systems. Research preprint mmlab@SIGS 6.2 Failure Patterns of the Evaluated Systems We read the measured cards of G0.5, InternW0 and GPT-6 Astra (Appendix E.4), together with the run logs of the agents. The overall pattern. Physical execution is the largest diagnosed failure group in all three systems, accounting for 41.4% of G0.5s failures, 37.2% of InternW0s, and 55.3% of GPT-6 Astras. GPT-6 Astras failures are particularly concentrated in execution, whereas G0.5 and InternW0 also show substantial perception and reasoning failures, at 27.7% and 32.8%, respectively; 611% of each systems failures occur while closing the loop. These proportions refer to the first unrecoverable error identified in each failed episode. The rule layer alone would overstate Mind-side errors for the end-to-end policies (Appendix Table 17), because scorer records reveal misremembered item more readily than video reveals motor fault. card therefore combines the layers. The dominant execution errors differ across systems. Failed or lost grasps are the most frequent errors for G0.5 and GPT-6 Astra, with 1,324 and 120 cases, while fine-control errors lead InternW0s profile with 1,132 cases. The two end-to-end policies also record 924 and 1,011 memory failures. These profiles identify distinct priorities: grasp reliability for G0.5 and GPT-6 Astra, fine control for InternW0, and task-state retention for both end-to-end policies. Differences across tasks. The dominant failure also varies by task, even within the same system. For G0.5, 202 of 300 bridge-building episodes (CP07) fail to grasp construction piece  (Fig. 13)  , making object acquisition the main obstacle to further progress. In light-cued pressing (DR2), however, 90 of 190 failures involve misread light (M-PERCEIVE) and 88 involve response that is not updated after the light changes (C-NO-UPDATE). Only eight concern the press itself or its timing. In incremental meal orders (P1), memory errors account for 210 of G0.5s 300 failed episodes and 245 of InternW0s 298 failed episodes. Where progress stops. No evaluated system completes whiteboard restoration (CP09) or bridge building (CP07), and failures on such workflows often occur before their reasoning stages are reached. On CP09, 299 of 300 G0.5 episodes stop before board removal. GPT-6 Astra fails during the lift in all 30 tray-carrying (DR4) episodes  (Fig. 15)  . Zero success on these tasks is therefore consistent with early physical bottlenecks rather than failures in downstream planning or repair. Most episodes fail in Mind or Act before closed-loop composition is tested. Analysis of budget use. Under the same decision budget, the agent logs show distinct termination patterns (Appendix Table 18). Gemini-4-Argon voluntarily stops in 829 of 900 episodes and uses approximately 33 decisions per episode. DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash uses 111.8 decisions on average, voluntarily stops in 385 episodes, and exhausts the decision and physics budgets in 286 and 94 episodes, respectively. GPT-6 Astra averages 79.6 decisions per episode. It voluntarily stops in 460 episodes, and only one of them succeeds, gate-passage episode (DR3) whose task was already complete when it stopped. The other 459 account for 77.9% of its 589 failed episodes, and in 264 of them the agent has used no more than 100 of the 150 allowed decisions. Among these 459 stops, the first unrecoverable error is attributed to execution in 289 cases, perception or reasoning in 127, and composition in 28. The remaining 15 cases fall outside these three capability groups. These results distinguish resource limits from the errors that prevent task completion. DeepSeek frequently exhausts its budget. GPT-6 Astra shows different pattern: many unsuccessful episodes end with substantial decision budget remaining, and execution errors dominate its voluntary stops, often after its motion planner rejects the requested poses. For episodes affected by execution errors, additional decisions are useful only if they enable effective retries or corrective actions  (Table 7)  . 6.3 From Failure Codes to Directions diagnosis helps model developer only if it says what to change, and the profiles narrow broad improvement goals to specific behaviors. Because each failure code names the step and the side of the Research preprint 26 mmlab@SIGS loop at which an episode broke, group of codes points to the capability that most needs to improve. An evaluation speaks most directly to two levers that developer can adjust without redesigning the model. One is the training data of an end-to-end policy. The other is the harness of an agent, that is, the tools and control loop through which it acts. Table 7 maps the three groups of the profile card, and the breakpoints shared by all of them, to such directions. The paragraphs below give the evidence behind each. Table 7. Directions for improvement by failure group. Grouped as on the profile card (Mind, Act and Composition). The directions concern the training data of end-to-end policies and the harness of agents. Evidence is from the measured cards of Appendix E.4 and the results of Section 5. Data: varied scenes and longer gaps between when information is shown and when it is needed Grasp, contact and timing: reliable grasps and fine contact, and responses within the windows of DR2 and DR3. Data: demonstrations weighted toward these segments, with more variation in pose, contact and timing. Harness: finer motion tools 761 precondition failures of InternW0, 271 of them on CP04, which heats the pot before all ingredients are in; agents that stop with budget left (Section 6.2) Checking and repairing outcomes: checking step before the next one and repairing it when it failed. Misremembered information is the most frequent Mind-side code of both measured end-to-end policies, with 924 failures of G0.5 and 1,011 of InternW0, and the VLAs lose 5972% of their Mind successes when the scene is randomized (Section 5.2). These failures point to maintaining task-relevant identities, order, and progress across operations, and to recognizing an item under new appearance. Closing this gap calls for data that stress what the failures expose, with varied scene appearance and longer gaps between the moment information is shown and the moment it is needed. Act failures: grasp, contact and timing. Failed or lost grasps account for 1,324 failures of G0.5 and fine-control errors for 1,132 of InternW0. On bridge building (CP07), 202 of 300 G0.5 episodes never grasp piece. G0.5s frequent grasp failures motivate training and control changes that improve contact acquisition and object retention. InternW0s fine-control errors motivate closer examination of action resolution and feedback during manipulation. Responses must also fall within the short windows of timed tasks such as the light-cued button (DR2) and the cyclic gates (DR3). On DR3, most failures of the two end-to-end policies come from the withdrawal after delivery rather than from the gate timing. The arm is still inside the gate corridor when the gate closes, or touches the gate while it closes. Demonstrations can be weighted toward these segments, with more variation in object pose, contact and timing, instead of being spread evenly over whole episodes. Composition failures: checking and repairing outcomes. InternW0 has 761 precondition failures, 271 of them on cooking (CP04), where it switches on the heat before all ingredients are in the pot. Each step is executed, but its outcome is not checked before the next one starts. Such failures call for checking whether the required physical state has been achieved before proceeding, and repairing step that failed. The scripted demonstrations show only steps that succeed, so policy never sees failed step followed by its repair. Recovery demonstrations can begin at frequently observed failures, such as slipped grasp or an incomplete placement, and show how to restore progress. Research preprint mmlab@SIGS Breakpoints: targeted data for end-to-end policies. These diagnoses also guide data collection. Because an end-to-end policy learns its behavior from demonstrations, the cards show where new data for it should be built. On whiteboard restoration (CP09), 299 of 300 G0.5 episodes end before the board is lifted off its stand, so the later stages of the task are never reached. Adding full-length demonstrations would spend most of their steps on later stages, which the policy almost never reaches. Demonstrations constructed around the breakpoint instead, starting from the states in which episodes stop and from perturbed states near them, concentrate the training data where the policy fails. Agents: the harness. For agents, the same codes also point to the harness. GPT-6 Astra breaks down mostly during execution and often stops after its motion planner rejects the requested poses (Section 6.2), so finer motion tools and retry step before stopping come first. Tool feedback should help distinguish an ineffective request from completed operation and support an appropriate retry or alternative action. The harness can also return the outcome of each step and require check before the next one, which addresses composition failures. It can also keep record of earlier failures, so that an agent recognizes breakpoint it has met before.

sections.title: 7 Limitations and Future Directions
sections.content: 7.1 Limitations Limited causal attribution. Each view is set of tasks, not an intervention on one system. Mind task still requires routine manipulation, an Act task still requires the robot to perceive its cue, and the Mind2Act workflows are longer than the single-view tasks and differ from them in content (Section 5.2). low Mind2Act result therefore cannot yet be separated from the effect of longer horizon or of an early execution error. The diagnosis harness attributes failures within each episode, where rules settle 22 to 38% of the failures of the three diagnosed systems and the LLM judge, with human review of uncertain cases, attributes the rest. Paused clock and fixed agent harness. Simulation pauses during inference, so timed tasks test whether an action is chosen and timed correctly in simulation time, not in real time (Section 5.2). The agents also receive an inverse-kinematics and motion-planning service and four times the physics budget of the end-to-end policies, and they are not trained on the benchmark. All three agents use the same fixed harness, so the results do not show what model would achieve with its own tools, controllers or memory. We therefore rank agents and end-to-end policies on separate leaderboards and treat the lead of the strongest agent as result under the paused clock rather than as real-time ability. Limited system coverage. The results cover three agents, four VLAs and two WAMs, and they include no hybrid or memory-augmented system. This is enough to compare the two families but too few for broader analysis, for example of how model size, training data or architecture shapes the results on Mind, Act and Mind2Act. Each agent is also evaluated on only ten episodes per task and level, so its results by difficulty level are coarse. Some episodes were run again after infrastructure failures (Appendix B). Limited embodiments and settings. All tasks are tabletop manipulation tasks in simulation on one bimanual platform with parallel grippers, and each task and level uses one fixed English instruction. Other embodiments and settings, such as dexterous hands, mobile manipulation, navigation and humanoid robots, are not yet covered. The Random setting changes appearance over wide range and is not meant to model deployment scene. Each capability category contains between one and six tasks, which is too few to support claims about single category. How the results in simulation relate to results on the physical robot has not yet been measured. 7.2 Future Directions We group the planned extensions into four directions that match the panels of Fig. 11, and the leaderboards will be updated with new systems, tasks and results as these extensions are added. The current views show where system fails, and the next step is to show why. On the Mind2Act tasks, an oracle for Mind will supply the task state that would otherwise have to be remembered or inferred, and an oracle for Act will let system call scripted skills for the physical operations. The gain from each oracle shows how much that capability contributes, and the gap that remains with both oracles shows the cost of composition. Each Mind2Act workflow will also be paired with the Mind and Act tasks that share its demands, and progress will be reported for each stage as the share of episodes that pass it among those that reach it, which removes the effect of horizon length. Matched pairs of runs that start from the same task state and differ only in whether the system receives feedback on grasp, placement or contact will then measure how much the outcome of an action guides the next decision. Broader and fairer comparison. The leaderboards will cover more systems and settings, so that the comparison between the two families no longer rests on one fixed setup. The task suite will also grow beyond tabletop bimanual manipulation to dexterous hands, mobile manipulation, navigation and humanoid robots, so that the three views can be tested on other embodiments. Human teleoperation and scripted expert acting through each interface will give every task reachable upper bound, and version of the protocol that adds inference time to the simulation clock will show how much of the agents result on timed tasks remains in real time. sandbox setting with its own leaderboard will let an agent bring its own harness, which runs in an isolated container with access only to the cameras, the robot state and joint-level control. The evaluated systems will extend to memory-augmented end-to-end policies, which test whether the weak memory of the VLAs comes from their architecture, and to hybrid systems that pair language-model planner with learned executor, which test whether combining the memory of the best agent with the practiced motions of the VLAs closes part of the gap. Repeated runs of the same instances will show how much results vary, together with the time and cost of each evaluation, and the difficulty levels of tasks on which the levels currently make no difference will be recalibrated. From diagnosis to better models. The diagnosis will move from explaining failures to guiding improvement. It will cover every evaluated system rather than three representative ones, and its rules and prompts will be released. The current harness reports only the first unrecoverable error of each episode, which shows where an episode breaks but not what happens after it. The diagnosis will therefore trace the Research preprint 29 mmlab@SIGS whole course of failed episode and record multiple breakpoints, including how an early error leads to later ones and whether the system notices mistake and recovers from it. Episodes will also start from verified intermediate states of the scripted demonstrations, so that each stage of workflow is measured even when an earlier stage fails. developer can then change model in response to its profile card and evaluate the new model on the same instances to check whether the change helped. Transfer to real robots. The last direction tests whether the findings hold outside simulation. Mind2Act World will add real-robot experiments in which its tasks are mapped to physical counterparts, starting with Mind2Act tasks such as CP02 and CP04 and extending to wider set of tasks, so that the Mind, Act and Mind2Act results can be verified on physical hardware. The same tasks will also be paired with similar tasks in other simulators, which shows how much of the failure analysis carries across platforms.

sections.title: 8 Conclusion
sections.content: We introduce Mind2Act World, benchmark that measures what robot retains and decides, how well it executes, and whether the two hold together when each physical outcome sets the next decision. Thirty tasks in three views, each with three difficulty levels and paired Clean and Random scenes, yield 180 configurations, all scored from physical outcomes by the same evaluator for agents and end-to-end policies. Our evaluation of three agents, four VLAs, and two WAMs over 56,700 episodes yields three main findings. First, the strongest agent leads every view without task-specific training, operating under paused clock and with motion planner, while the four fine-tuned VLAs have similar Overall success rates and differ mainly in the tasks they handle best. Second, single-view ability does not carry over to Mind2Act tasks: the best system falls from 52.7% on Mind and 39.0% on Act to 12.0% on Mind2Act, and no end-to-end policy exceeds 3.6%. Third, the VLAs are limited even before composition, by memory that mostly disappears when the scene changes and by the first physical contact of the longer workflows. Eight of the thirty tasks are completed by no system. In current embodied systems, they remain Wang Yangming held that knowing and acting are one. separate abilities, unevenly developed and not yet joined. Mind2Act World makes the distance between them measurable. The interventions, references and additional systems described in Section 7 are our next steps toward explaining it.

sections.title: Appendix Overview
sections.content: The appendices give the material needed to rebuild and use the benchmark. Appendices AC describe the platform, protocol and systems, Appendix reports results by task and setting with confidence intervals, Appendix gives the diagnostic details, and Appendix is the reference for the thirty tasks. Appendix A, Simulation platform and data: the simulator, assets and parallel evaluation, how demonstrations are collected and qualified, and how Clean and Random test instances are generated. Appendix B, Evaluation protocol: what system observes and how it acts, episode horizons and budgets, how the task score is computed, and how results are selected and kept comparable. Appendix C, Systems and training: the initialization, global batch size and training steps of each evaluated end-to-end policy, and the API setting of the agents. Appendix D, Detailed results: outcomes by setting, success counts with confidence intervals, scores and success rates for every task, and successes by difficulty level. Appendix E, Diagnostic details: how failed episode is assigned to stage and code, task-level results by view, the share of failures settled by each layer, the model profile cards of three representative systems, the stop reasons of the agent runs, and the behavioral profiles. Appendix F, Task details: the real-world needs behind the tasks, summary table and the task cards.

sections.title: A Simulation Platform and Data Details
sections.content: This appendix complements Section 4.1 with the details needed to rebuild the task scenes and to regenerate the demonstration data. A.1 Simulation Platform Mind2Act World runs in Isaac Sim with two ARX X5 arms and parallel grippers. fixed head camera and two wrist cameras provide RGB images. Physics is stepped at 120 Hz and robot targets are updated at 30 Hz. Simulation pauses while model computes, so task deadlines are measured in simulation time and cost in wall-clock time. Each task is defined by specification that fixes the scene, the objects and mechanisms, the per-level parameters, the episode randomization and the evaluator. Changing the level or the seed changes only these parameters, never the objective or the scoring rule. A.2 Assets and Parallel Evaluation As shown in Fig. 7, task scenes combine shared robot and workspace assets with task-specific objects, instruments, and mechanisms. Their geometry, motion, and contact properties are configured so that every required effect is physically realized: button travels and releases, dial retains its reading after release, cloth stays folded only if it is laid flat, and balance beam deflects under the actual load. Physical completion checks compare simulator states and events with task requirements, including release and support after placement. Episodes run in isolated simulator processes. scheduler distributes task-level conditions across the available GPUs and checks the first result of each condition before launching its remaining seeds. valid policy failure lets evaluation continue, whereas runtime failure blocks the remaining seeds for inspection. Model services may persist across episodes, and requests from concurrent episodes are kept apart, so that each episode observes its own visual-action sequence. A.3 Demonstration Collection Demonstrations are collected under one protocol for every task and level: 50 episodes per task and level for all thirty tasks (4,500 in total), all recorded in Clean scenes. Each episode records the instruction, three RGB streams at 30 Hz, and the joint states, with joint targets logged at 120 Hz. demonstration Research preprint 35 mmlab@SIGS Table 8. A.4 Instance Generation: Clean and Random Settings Every task and level has frozen set of 50 evaluation slots, and each slot can be run in two settings that share the task instance and differ only in the scene around it. Each setting counts as separate configuration, so the thirty tasks, three levels and two settings give the 180 configurations of the benchmark. Research preprint 36 mmlab@SIGS Evaluation seeds are not used for training. Clean. The slots task seed draws the task-relevant parameters described in Section 3.5.1: object layouts, initial and target states, event orders and hidden parameters such as the PR5 stamp angle. sections.title: B Evaluation Protocol Details
sections.content: With the scenes and test instances fixed by Appendix A, this appendix specifies how system interacts with them, expanding Section 4: what it observes and how it acts, how long an episode may run, how the episode is scored, and how results are selected. B.1 Observations, Actions and Hidden State policy receives the task instruction, the selected RGB cameras with arm joint positions and the declared gripper state, and earlier public observations and permitted feedback. Hidden task state is excluded, including unannounced targets and tolerances such as the PR5 angle, the DR3 gate timing and the DR4 drift radius. The evaluator uses it only to check contact, support, timing and completion. End-to-end policies predict joint or end-effector actions. Joint predictions are denormalized and relative offsets converted to absolute targets. Cartesian poses are transformed into the controller frame and mapped to joint targets by inverse kinematics. Each policy executes its configured chunk before predicting again. Agents instead select Cartesian targets through motion tools, which local inverse-kinematics and motion-planning service turns into trajectories using declared robot and fixed-scene geometry. Depth and pixel-to-world queries are disabled, and agents may retrieve earlier public images without advancing the simulation. The planner, history access and any adapter fallback are therefore part of the evaluated system  (Table 9)  . Table 9. System interfaces. What each system family receives and returns under the shared protocol. Family Input Output Must disclose VLA / WAM Instruction, 13 RGB views, Joint or EEF action chunk Agent Hybrid joint state Instruction, RGB, history, tool feedback As above, split across modules Motion-tool calls Planner calls and controller actions Checkpoint, chunk, control period, data Model, harness, tools, budget, latency Module boundaries, fallbacks, cost Not available to any system: hidden targets and tolerances, gate timing, drift radii, depth and pixel-to-world queries. Research preprint 37 mmlab@SIGS B.2 Horizons and Budgets The end-to-end task horizon uses the 90th percentile of demonstration duration at each level, multiplied by 1.2 and rounded up to control step. Clean and Random share it. Agents use this physics budget multiplied by four and at most 150 decisions per episode  (Table 10)  . Rejected and invalid actions count as decisions. Network retries do not, with up to 12 retries per decision. An agent episode ends when the task is complete, when the agent stops, or when either budget is used. Wall-clock limits are safety stops. An episode stopped by one is scored like any other unfinished episode. Table 10. Run budgets. 𝐵 denotes the taskand level-specific end-to-end budget in physics steps. Leaderboard Physics steps Decisions Wall-clock safety limit End-to-end Agent 𝐵 4𝐵 unlimited 150 2 hours 6 hours B.3 Task Score The task evaluator produces score between 0 and 100 using the task-specific rule shown on the task pages of the project website. successful episode scores 100. Any other outcome receives the partial credit defined for that task, or zero. For example, CP01 gives credit for each requested item released into the correct tray and remaining supported, and full success additionally requires every order to be complete and the meal trays to be retrieved. Partial-credit scales differ between tasks, so scores are compared across systems on one task and averaged within view, but not compared across tasks. For each task, the evaluator marks an episode as successful when it meets all completion criteria, satisfies any prerequisites, and violates no rule that prevents success. We calculate each systems success rate by dividing the number of episodes marked as successful by the total number of evaluated episodes. B.4 Evaluation Integrity and Result Selection Every system on leaderboard receives the same frozen list of task, level and seed instances. Reset restores the robot, objects, task stage, evaluator and random state, and clears policy memory. Each episode writes manifest that binds the task, level, seed and configuration hashes to the observation profile, action interface, model or checkpoint version, clocks, budgets, termination reason and scorer output, together with an event record that separates the issued action from the evaluators completion check. All evaluations in this report were run by the benchmark team on its own machines. Retained attempts. Each system receives one result per test instance and scene setting. Infrastructure failures can trigger retry. valid run in which the policy fails the task still counts as failure. Earlier attempts may remain in the logs for cost tracking, but each retained result counts only once.

Research preprint 40 mmlab@SIGS E.1 Diagnostic Steps and Failure Codes For each failed episode, we look for the first error from which the system could no longer recover. An error that the system later corrects does not count. We assign the failure to the earliest stage that explains the observed outcome. For example, choosing the wrong object to grasp is reasoning error. Choosing the correct object but failing to hold it is an execution error. We defined the failure codes by mapping the steps of each of the 30 tasks and identifying what could go wrong at each step. Table 15 lists the resulting 21 codes. Eighteen describe failures in four stages: perceiving the scene and reasoning about the next action (Mind), executing the action (Act), and checking its physical outcome to decide what to do next (Mind-Action composition). The remaining three codes apply to the episode as whole: the system exhausts its physics or decision budget, stalls or repeats an action, or leaves too little evidence to identify the failure. These codes are not assigned to side. Each task uses only the codes relevant to its steps. The side of failure (Mind, Act or composition) follows from its stage, whatever the view of the task. misread cue in an Act task counts as Mind failure. The assignment is classification of the first unrecoverable error and is not causal test. Table 15. Failure codes used in episode diagnosis. The table groups 18 codes by the stage at which the failure occurs. Three episode-level codes cover an exhausted budget, stalled or repeated actions, and insufficient evidence. Success is concentrated in few tasks. For three of the four VLAs, one task, passing through gates that open and close on cycle (DR3), accounts for 3641% of all successes: 238 of 628 for KinRT, 236 of 574 for 𝜋0.5 and 227 of 626 for X-VLA. For X-VLA, three tasks (DR3, cloth folding PR4 and resistance adjustment PR1) account for 549 of its 626 successes. Gemini-4-Argon shows the same pattern on smaller scale: resistance adjustment and gate passage together contribute 24 of its 42 successes. Eight tasks are completed by no system. Workpiece tracking (M1), tray carrying with loose balls (DR4), oriented stamping (PR5), the domino chain (PR6), moving-rack loading (CP03), temperature-controlled cooking (CP04), bridge building (CP07) and whiteboard restoration (CP09) have no successful episode among the 56,700. On four of them (DR4, PR6, CP07 and CP09), every system also has mean task Research preprint 41 mmlab@SIGS score of zero, meaning that not even the first scored stage is reached. Each of these tasks has fifty scripted demonstrations per level that pass the same evaluator, confirming platform feasibility. Mind End-to-end policies. The VLAs complete few Mind episodes, and their successes are concentrated in narrow set of tasks. KinRTs 132 Mind successes include 46 on steamer-stack restoration (P2), 22 on card matching (M2), and 20 on repeated-item recognition (E1). Of the 105 successes of 𝜋0.5, 43 are on P2 and 22 on hazard navigation (S2). These successes occur mostly at the Easy level, where the least information must be retained (Table 14 for 𝜋0.5 and G0.5), and mostly in Clean scenes (Section 5.2). Across the four VLAs, workpiece tracking (M1) is never completed and tray-layout restoration (S1) only once. policy that conditions on the current observation or on short history cannot recover information that has left its view, and the Mind results of the VLAs are consistent with this limitation. Evaluating memory-augmented policies [29, 30, 56] on the Mind view provides direct test. Agents. GPT-6 Astra succeeds in 52.7% of Mind episodes, but its performance is uneven within three of the five categories: 100% on hazard navigation (S2) against 23.3% on tray-layout restoration (S1), 93.3% on card matching (M2) against 0% on workpiece tracking (M1), and 43.3% on meal orders (P1) against 0% on steamer-stack restoration (P2). The tasks it solves best are those in which the action is button press or simple placement (S2, F1, M2, E2, E1), whereas the tasks it fails additionally require lifting covers, routing workpiece through stations, or unstacking and restacking baskets. Its Mind score therefore reflects the reach of its motion tools as well as its memory, and because each category contains only two tasks, category-level differences should not be read as differences between kinds of memory. DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash shows the same pattern on smaller scale: its 33 Mind successes all come from five of these tasks (M2 10, E1 6, E2 6, S2 6 and F1 5). Gemini-4-Argon obtains its 13 on six tasks. Act End-to-end policies. Act is the view in which the VLAs succeed most often, and their success comes mainly from dynamic response. Averaged over tasks, the four VLAs reach 2228% on the four dynamic tasks and 418% on the six precision tasks. Although they are trained on the same demonstration collection, the policies differ sharply from task to task, and no single policy leads throughout: G0.5 leads on DR1 and DR2, KinRT on DR3, and X-VLA on PR1 and PR4. G0.5 leads light-cued response (DR2, 110 of 300 episodes) but is last on resistance adjustment (PR1, 9), where X-VLA leads with 130. X-VLA also completes 192 cloth-folding episodes (PR4), against 30 to 54 for the other three. Apart from the zero-success tasks DR4, PR5 and PR6, pen tracing (PR3) is completed only three times in 1,200 VLA episodes. Agents. GPT-6 Astra completes every resistance-adjustment episode and most episodes of the three timed tasks DR1, DR2, and DR3 (76.7%, 90.0%, and 80.0%), yet it completes no episode of the five tasks that require continuous contact or carried load (DR4, PR3, PR4, PR5, and PR6). The Hard level of DR2 allows 2.6 to press lit button, whereas the agents mean request time on Act tasks is 9.2 s. Because simulation pauses during inference, the agent can still meet the deadline. These results show that the agent selects and times actions correctly in simulation time. They do not test real-time reaction. At Easy, CP01 has single order and CP06 single item to weigh, so little must be remembered and practiced motion carries most of the task. For these policies, the two workflows then behave much like Act tasks. InternW0 departs from this pattern: block structure from shown blueprint (CP08) contributes 35 of its 91 Mind2Act successes, more than any other end-to-end policy completes on that task, while produce weighing (CP06) contributes 48. Mind2Act workflows mostly fail early. On the four workflows that no system completes (CP03, CP04, CP07 and CP09), the mean task score of every system is at most 1.2 points out of 100. The profile card of G0.5  (Fig. 13)  shows why for one policy: 202 of its 300 bridge-building episodes (CP07) never grasp piece. Elsewhere, partial credit adds little. For every system, the Mind2Act score exceeds the success rate by at most 1.5 points, so under the current scoring rules failed Mind2Act episode has usually failed early rather than near completion. For most systems evaluated here, these four workflows therefore end at the first physical step, before the composition they were designed to test. InternW0 on cooking (CP04) is the exception: in 271 of its 300 episodes it switches on the heat before all ingredients are in the pot, which is composition error. What the view-level comparison shows. Conveyor meal assembly (CP01) reuses the conveyor interception of DR1 and, like P1, depends on remembered food orders. Yet GPT-6 Astra completes CP01 more often (60.0%) than P1 (43.3%), and every VLA that completes any CP01 episode does so more often than the product of its P1 and DR1 rates would predict (8.0% for KinRT against 0.1%). Mind2Act task is thus not simply the conjunction of two single-view tasks, and lower Mind2Act score cannot by itself be attributed to composition. The views instead show narrower finding: each systems ability is uneven across Mind and Act, the systems differ in which is weaker, and every system succeeds less often on the Mind2Act workflows than on its stronger single view. As in MBTI, the first and last letters sort the codes into four families. Feedforward Planners (I J) think more than they do and stick to plan made in advance. Feedback Adapters (I P) think more than they do and correct course step by step. Procedural Executors (E J) do more than they think and follow fixed routine. Servo Responders (E P) have steady hands that adjust as the scene changes. The middle letters add the details: what the system remembers better (S or N) and whether its hands are more accurate (T) or more timely (F). Since every end-to-end policy evaluated here succeeds more often on Act than on Mind  (Table 4)  , all of them start with E, while GPT-6 Astra starts with I. Meet the three diagnosed systems. InternW0 is an ENFP, Goalkeeper among the Servo Responders, and holds all four letters firmly: it succeeds more often on Act than on Mind (17.6% against 5.4%), on spatial than on entity memory (5.3% against 0.2%), on dynamic response than on precise execution (31.8% against 8.1%), and on feedback-driven than on plan-driven workflows (5.6% against 0.5%). G0.5 is an ENFP too, though only just on the memory and lifestyle letters (0.0% against 0.8%, and 2.1% against 2.5%). GPT-6 Astra is an ISFJ, Dispatcher among the Feedforward Planners: Mind-led (52.7% against 39.0% on Act), better at entity than spatial memory (68.3% against 61.7%), more successful on dynamic response than on precise execution (61.7% against 23.9%, though its says only that the timed tasks go Research preprint 49 mmlab@SIGS better than the precision tasks, not that it reacts fast), and better on plan-driven than on feedback-driven workflows (16.0% against 8.0%). In short, the two Goalkeepers do relatively best on dynamic response, and the Dispatcher completes plan-driven workflows twice as often as feedback-driven ones.

sections.content: This appendix is the reference for the tasks. It explains where they come from, what each one asks, and how it gets harder. Mind tasks emphasize retaining information and selecting actions, Act tasks emphasize physical precision and timely response, and Mind2Act tasks combine remembered or inferred task state with execution outcomes that constrain subsequent actions. Table 20 lists all thirty tasks. Every task has 50 demonstrations per level (4,500 in total) and is covered by all nine evaluated systems  (Table 5)  . The three levels describe changes in task demands rather than calibrated difficulty ranking. Demonstration and evaluation seeds are disjoint. The common observation and scoring protocol in Section 4 applies throughout. F.1 From Real-World Requirements to Tasks Each task is built from requirement that makes real activity hard for robot.
